## What you will learn

- Convert between degrees, radians, revolutions and RPM without looking anything up.
- Explain why robotics software (and ROS) uses radians.
- Use arc length $s = r\theta$ and rim speed $v = \omega r$ for wheels and turning robots.
- Wrap any angle to $(-\pi, \pi]$ and compute the shortest difference between two headings.
- Avoid the classic angle bugs: the 350° error, naive averaging and the −π/π edge.

## Why it matters

A robot's heading is an angle. So is each joint of an arm, the direction of every LiDAR beam and the reading of a gyroscope. [01.12](../../01-first-robot/01.12-encoder-distance-and-square.md) turns the robot by exactly 90°. [05.02](../../05-frames-and-transforms/05.02-pose-in-2d.md) represents the robot pose as $(x, y, \theta)$ and relies on angle wrapping. [08.10](../../08-control/08.10-straight-line-heading-control.md) and [08.11](../../08-control/08.11-rotate-exactly-90.md) control heading. [07.05](../../07-sensors/07.05-imu-fundamentals.md) integrates gyro rates in rad/s. [FM.03](FM.03-trigonometry.md) builds trigonometry on top of this.

The most common heading-controller bug in hobby robots is a robot facing 170° that is told to face −170°. It turns 340° the long way around instead of 20° the short way. This lesson makes that bug impossible for you.

## Concept

An angle measures an amount of turning. You already know **degrees**: a full turn is 360°, a number picked by the Babylonians because it divides nicely.

A **radian** is not arbitrary. Take a circle of radius $r$. Walk along its edge a distance equal to $r$. The angle you swept is one radian. A full circle has circumference $2\pi r$, so a full turn is $2\pi$ radians, about 6.283.

Why bother? Radians connect turning to distance directly. A wheel of radius 0.045 m that turns 2 rad moves its rim $0.045 \times 2 = 0.09$ m. In degrees you would need a conversion factor in every formula. Every derivative of sin and cos, every physics equation and every ROS message assumes radians ([REP-103](https://www.ros.org/reps/rep-0103.html)). Degrees are for humans reading logs. Radians are for code.

Angles also **wrap around**. Heading 350° and heading −10° are the same direction. Computers store a plain float, which doesn't know this. You must teach it, or your robot will take the long way around.

> [!TIP]
> **Ask your teacher:** "Show me three real bugs caused by angle wrapping in robot code, and how wrap-to-pi fixes each one."

## Technical explanation

### Level 1 — Intuition: direction on a dial

Picture the robot from above. It faces along its $x$ axis (forward). Turning **left (counter-clockwise) is positive**, turning right is negative. This is the right-hand rule around the $z$ axis pointing up (REP-103). So:

- 0 = facing along $+x$ (east on a map)
- $+\pi/2$ (+90°) = facing $+y$ (north, or "left" of the start)
- $\pm\pi$ (±180°) = facing $-x$
- $-\pi/2$ (−90°) = facing $-y$

### Level 2 — Practical conversions

$$\theta_{\text{rad}} = \theta_{\text{deg}} \cdot \frac{\pi}{180}, \qquad \theta_{\text{deg}} = \theta_{\text{rad}} \cdot \frac{180}{\pi}$$

1 rad = 57.2958°, and 1° = 0.0174533 rad. Values worth memorizing:

| Degrees | 30 | 45 | 60 | 90 | 180 | 360 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Radians | $\pi/6$ = 0.5236 | $\pi/4$ = 0.7854 | $\pi/3$ = 1.0472 | $\pi/2$ = 1.5708 | $\pi$ = 3.1416 | $2\pi$ = 6.2832 |

**Angular speed** is angle per time, in rad/s. Motor datasheets use RPM (revolutions per minute):

$$\omega_{\text{rad/s}} = \text{RPM} \cdot \frac{2\pi}{60}$$

karmel's motor is rated 205 RPM with no load: $205 \cdot 2\pi/60 = 21.47$ rad/s.

**Encoder resolution** in angle: 2464 ticks per wheel revolution means $2\pi/2464 = 0.00255$ rad = 0.146° per tick.

### Level 3 — Mathematics: arc length, rim speed, wrapping

**Arc length.** By the definition of the radian, an arc of angle $\theta$ on a circle of radius $r$ has length

$$s = r\theta$$

Differentiate with respect to time (see [FM.17](FM.17-derivatives.md)) and you get **rim speed**, the speed of a point at distance $r$ from the axis:

$$v = \omega r$$

The wheel rim at 21.47 rad/s moves at $21.47 \cdot 0.045 = 0.966$ m/s. For a robot turning in place, each wheel is $L/2 = 0.1$ m from the center. A 90° turn moves each wheel along an arc of $s = 0.1 \cdot \pi/2 = 0.157$ m. A LiDAR beam 1° apart at 5 m range lands $5 \cdot 0.01745 = 0.087$ m from its neighbor. That is why distant walls look sparse in a scan.

These formulas **only work in radians**. With degrees, $s = r\theta$ is wrong by a factor of 57.3.

**Wrapping.** Every angle $\theta$ is equivalent to $\theta + 2\pi k$ for any integer $k$. We pick one representative in the half-open interval $(-\pi, \pi]$. Mathematically:

$$\operatorname{wrap}(\theta) = \theta - 2\pi \left\lceil \frac{\theta - \pi}{2\pi} \right\rceil$$

Numbers: $\operatorname{wrap}(340°) = \operatorname{wrap}(5.934) = 5.934 - 2\pi \lceil 0.444 \rceil = 5.934 - 6.283 = -0.349$ rad = −20°. And $\operatorname{wrap}(7.0) = 7.0 - 2\pi\lceil 0.614 \rceil = 0.717$ rad.

Why $(-\pi, \pi]$ and not $[0, 2\pi)$? Because heading **errors** should be small numbers with a sign. The sign says which way to turn, and zero is "on target".

**Shortest angular difference.** The error from current heading $\theta_c$ to target $\theta_t$ is

$$e = \operatorname{wrap}(\theta_t - \theta_c)$$

With $\theta_t = 170°$ and $\theta_c = -170°$: the naive difference is $340°$, which means turn left almost a full circle. The wrapped difference is $-20°$, which means turn right 20°. A P-controller multiplies this error by a gain, so the naive version doesn't only take the long way. It also commands a turn rate 17 times too large.

**Averaging angles.** The naive mean of 179° and −179° is 0°, pointing exactly the wrong way. The correct average direction is 180°. Average the unit vectors $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ and convert back with atan2. That uses [FM.03](FM.03-trigonometry.md) and [FM.05](FM.05-vectors.md).

### Level 4 — Implementation

Three ways to wrap in Python, with their edge cases:

| Method | $\pi$ | $-\pi$ | $3\pi$ | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `(a + pi) % (2*pi) - pi` | **−π** | −π | −π | range is $[-\pi, \pi)$, so +π flips sign |
| `atan2(sin(a), cos(a))` | π | −π | 3.1415926535897927 | tiny float noise; also 2π → −2.4e-16 |
| `fmod` with an edge fix (below) | π | **π** | π | exactly $(-\pi, \pi]$ |

For control, the −π/π difference rarely matters, because both mean "turn around". It matters for **tests and comparisons**, like `assert wrap(a) == expected` or deduplicating headings. Pick one function, put it in one module (the course keeps it in `labs/python/robotlab/geometry.py`) and use it everywhere.

## Diagram

```text
                 +y  (θ = +π/2 = +90°)
                  ▲
                  │        positive = counter-clockwise (left turn)
                  │    ╭──╮
     θ = ±π  ◄────┼────┼──┼──────► +x  (θ = 0, robot forward)
     (±180°)      │    ╰──╯
                  │
                  ▼
                 −y  (θ = −π/2 = −90°)

 Radian = the angle whose arc length equals the radius:

        ╭──── arc s = r ────╮
       ╱                     ╲
      ╱   θ = 1 rad ≈ 57.3°   ●
      ●───────── r ──────────╯
   center

 Wrapping: 170° → −170°

   naive  e = −170 − 170 = −340°  (turn right almost a full circle)
   wrap(e) = +20°                 (turn left 20°)

         target −170° ●╲
                        ╲ 20°
                ────────── ● robot at 170°
```

## Code

Save as `fm02_angles.py` and run `python fm02_angles.py`. Only the standard library is needed.

```python
"""FM.02 — angle conversions, wrapping and shortest differences."""
import math

TWO_PI = 2.0 * math.pi


def wrap_to_pi(angle_rad: float) -> float:
    """Wrap an angle to the half-open interval (-pi, pi]."""
    w = math.fmod(angle_rad + math.pi, TWO_PI)   # fmod keeps the sign of the dividend
    if w <= 0.0:
        w += TWO_PI
    return w - math.pi


def angle_diff(target_rad: float, current_rad: float) -> float:
    """Signed shortest rotation that takes `current` to `target`."""
    return wrap_to_pi(target_rad - current_rad)


def mean_angle(angles_rad: list[float]) -> float:
    """Circular mean: average the unit vectors, then take the direction."""
    s = sum(math.sin(a) for a in angles_rad)
    c = sum(math.cos(a) for a in angles_rad)
    return math.atan2(s, c)


def rpm_to_rad_s(rpm: float) -> float:
    return rpm * TWO_PI / 60.0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"90 deg = {math.radians(90):.4f} rad, 1 rad = {math.degrees(1):.4f} deg")
    print(f"205 RPM = {rpm_to_rad_s(205):.2f} rad/s -> rim {rpm_to_rad_s(205) * 0.045:.3f} m/s")
    print(f"per encoder tick: {TWO_PI / 2464:.5f} rad = {math.degrees(TWO_PI / 2464):.3f} deg")

    for a in (math.pi, -math.pi, 3 * math.pi, math.radians(340), 7.0, -7.0, TWO_PI):
        naive = (a + math.pi) % TWO_PI - math.pi
        print(f"a={a:9.5f}  wrap_to_pi={wrap_to_pi(a):9.5f}  naive%={naive:9.5f}")

    e = angle_diff(math.radians(-170), math.radians(170))
    print(f"heading error 170 -> -170 deg: {math.degrees(e):.1f} deg")
    print(f"mean of 179 and -179 deg: naive {(179 - 179) / 2:.1f}, circular "
          f"{math.degrees(mean_angle([math.radians(179), math.radians(-179)])):.1f}")

    # a few assertions that document the contract
    assert wrap_to_pi(math.pi) == math.pi
    assert wrap_to_pi(-math.pi) == math.pi
    assert abs(wrap_to_pi(math.radians(725)) - math.radians(5)) < 1e-12
    print("all assertions passed")
```

Output:

```text
90 deg = 1.5708 rad, 1 rad = 57.2958 deg
205 RPM = 21.47 rad/s -> rim 0.966 m/s
per encoder tick: 0.00255 rad = 0.146 deg
a=  3.14159  wrap_to_pi=  3.14159  naive%= -3.14159
a= -3.14159  wrap_to_pi=  3.14159  naive%= -3.14159
a=  9.42478  wrap_to_pi=  3.14159  naive%= -3.14159
a=  5.93412  wrap_to_pi= -0.34907  naive%= -0.34907
a=  7.00000  wrap_to_pi=  0.71681  naive%=  0.71681
a= -7.00000  wrap_to_pi= -0.71681  naive%= -0.71681
a=  6.28319  wrap_to_pi=  0.00000  naive%=  0.00000
heading error 170 -> -170 deg: -20.0 deg
```

With numpy (used from [05.02](../../05-frames-and-transforms/05.02-pose-in-2d.md) on), the same wrap works on whole arrays. `np.fmod` plus `np.where` replace the `if`.

## Exercise

All exercises need hardware: none.

### Exercise FM.02-E1 — Conversions `[numerical]`

Convert by hand, then check with Python: (a) 15° to rad, (b) 2.5 rad to degrees, (c) karmel's software turn-rate limit of 2.5 rad/s to degrees per second and to RPM of the robot body, (d) a gyro reading of 0.5 rad/s held for 3 s to the total degrees turned.

### Exercise FM.02-E2 — Wrap these `[numerical]`

Wrap to $(-\pi, \pi]$ and give the answer in radians and in degrees: (a) 5.0 rad, (b) −4.0 rad, (c) 10.0 rad, (d) −190°, (e) 725°.

### Exercise FM.02-E3 — Predict the naive modulo `[predict]`

**Before running**, predict what `(a + math.pi) % (2*math.pi) - math.pi` returns for `a = math.pi`. Is it in $(-\pi, \pi]$? Then predict what `math.atan2(math.sin(a), math.cos(a))` returns for `a = 2*math.pi`. Run both and explain.

### Exercise FM.02-E4 — Heading controller error `[coding]`

A proportional heading controller commands $\omega = K_p \cdot e$ with $K_p = 2.0$, clamped to ±2.5 rad/s. Write `turn_rate(target_rad, current_rad)` that uses `angle_diff`. Evaluate it for (target, current) = (90°, −135°), (−170°, 170°) and (10°, 5°). Then compute what the **naive** error (no wrapping) would command for the first two cases.

### Exercise FM.02-E5 — Arc lengths for karmel `[numerical]`

karmel turns in place by 135°. Wheel separation is $L = 0.200$ m and wheel radius is $r = 0.045$ m. How far does each wheel's contact point travel along the floor, and through what angle (in radians) does each wheel rotate?

## Expected result

- **FM.02-E1:** (a) $15\pi/180 = $ **0.2618 rad**; (b) **143.24°**; (c) **143.2 °/s**, which is $2.5 \cdot 60/(2\pi) = $ **23.9 RPM** of the robot body; (d) $1.5$ rad = **85.9°**.
- **FM.02-E2:** (a) **−1.2832 rad (−73.5°)**; (b) **2.2832 rad (130.8°)**; (c) **−2.5664 rad (−147.0°)**; (d) **170°** = 2.9671 rad; (e) **5°** = 0.0873 rad.
- **FM.02-E3:** The naive modulo returns **−3.14159…** (−π). $(\pi + \pi) \bmod 2\pi = 0$, then $0 - \pi = -\pi$, which is outside $(-\pi, \pi]$. The atan2 trick returns about **−2.45e-16**, not exactly 0, because `sin(2π)` is not exactly zero in floating point.
- **FM.02-E4:** (90°, −135°): the wrapped error is −135° = −2.356 rad, so $\omega = -4.71$, clamped to **−2.5 rad/s**, turning right. Naive: error +225° = 3.927 rad → **+2.5 rad/s**, the long way. (−170°, 170°): wrapped +20° = +0.349 rad → **+0.698 rad/s**, a gentle left turn. Naive: −340° = −5.934 rad → clamped **−2.5 rad/s**, a full-speed right turn the long way around. (10°, 5°): **+0.175 rad/s** in both versions.
- **FM.02-E5:** Arc $s = (L/2)\theta = 0.1 \cdot 2.3562 = $ **0.2356 m** per wheel, in opposite directions. Wheel rotation $= s/r = $ **5.236 rad** (= 300°) per wheel.

<details><summary>Reference solution for FM.02-E4</summary>

```python
import math


def wrap_to_pi(a: float) -> float:
    w = math.fmod(a + math.pi, 2 * math.pi)
    if w <= 0.0:
        w += 2 * math.pi
    return w - math.pi


def turn_rate(target_rad: float, current_rad: float, kp: float = 2.0, limit: float = 2.5) -> float:
    e = wrap_to_pi(target_rad - current_rad)
    return max(-limit, min(limit, kp * e))


for t_deg, c_deg in ((90, -135), (-170, 170), (10, 5)):
    t, c = math.radians(t_deg), math.radians(c_deg)
    naive = max(-2.5, min(2.5, 2.0 * (t - c)))
    print(f"{t_deg:5d} {c_deg:5d}  wrapped={turn_rate(t, c):+.3f}  naive={naive:+.3f}")
```
</details>

## Troubleshooting

### Symptom: the robot spins the long way around (or oscillates wildly) near ±180°

1. **Log the heading error**, not just the heading. If it ever exceeds $\pi$ in magnitude, you are not wrapping the difference.
2. **Check where you wrap.** Wrap the *difference* $\theta_t - \theta_c$. Wrapping only the two inputs is not enough, because their difference can still be up to $2\pi$.
3. **Check the units.** An error of "90" means degrees leaked into a radian controller. Grep for `degrees(`/`radians(` near sensor input.
4. **Check the sign convention.** If the robot turns away from the target consistently, one source (IMU, odometry, a simulator) uses clockwise-positive. REP-103 is counter-clockwise-positive.

### Symptom: a test comparing angles fails for "equal" angles

1. Print both with `repr()`. Is one π and the other −π? Wrap both with the same function, or compare `abs(wrap_to_pi(a - b)) < tol`.
2. Is the difference around 1e-16? That is floating-point noise. Never use `==` on computed angles. Use a tolerance.

## Common mistakes

- **Passing degrees to `math.sin`/`np.cos`.** Every math library expects radians. It happens because humans configure in degrees. Convert at the boundary and name variables `_deg` / `_rad`.
- **Wrapping inputs but not the difference.** See Troubleshooting.
- **Averaging angles arithmetically.** It gives wrong results near ±π. Use the circular mean.
- **Integrating heading without wrapping, then comparing.** Accumulated yaw of 12 rad is a valid internal state (sometimes useful to count turns), but wrap before you compare or publish it.
- **Using RPM or deg/s in kinematics.** $v = \omega r$ needs rad/s.

## Knowledge check

1. What is one radian, geometrically, and how many are in a full turn?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   The angle whose arc length equals the radius. A full turn is $2\pi \approx 6.283$ rad.
   </details>

2. A wheel of radius 0.035 m spins at 300 RPM. What is its rim speed?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   $\omega = 300 \cdot 2\pi/60 = 31.42$ rad/s, so $v = \omega r = 31.42 \cdot 0.035 = 1.10$ m/s.
   </details>

3. Wrap −3.5 rad to $(-\pi, \pi]$.
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   $-3.5 + 2\pi = 2.783$ rad (159.5°).
   </details>

4. Predict: a heading controller computes `error = target - current` without wrapping. The robot is at −179° and the target is 179°. What does the robot do?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   The error is +358°, so it turns left with maximum rate almost a full circle, instead of turning 2° right. If the gain is high it may overshoot and repeat.
   </details>

5. Why does ROS use $(-\pi, \pi]$ rather than $[0, 2\pi)$ for yaw differences?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Because the error then has a meaningful sign (which way to turn) and zero is centered. With $[0, 2\pi)$, "a little bit to the right" would be about 6.2, a large number.
   </details>

6. Debugging: the average of two IMU yaw readings, 3.13 rad and −3.13 rad, comes out as 0. Why, and what is the fix?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Both readings point almost exactly backward (±179.3°). Their arithmetic mean is 0 (forward). Use the circular mean `atan2(sum(sin), sum(cos))`, which gives ±π.
   </details>

7. An encoder has 2464 ticks per revolution on a wheel of radius 0.045 m. What linear distance does one tick represent?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   $\Delta\theta = 2\pi/2464 = 0.00255$ rad, so $s = r\Delta\theta = 0.045 \cdot 0.00255 = 0.000115$ m = 0.115 mm.
   </details>

## Practical challenge

Write `angles.py` with `wrap_to_pi`, `angle_diff` and `mean_angle`, plus a pytest file with property-style tests over 10,000 random angles in $[-100, 100]$ rad:

- `wrap_to_pi(a)` is always in $(-\pi, \pi]$.
- `cos`/`sin` of `wrap_to_pi(a)` equal those of `a` within 1e-9.
- `abs(angle_diff(t, c)) <= pi`, and `wrap_to_pi(c + angle_diff(t, c))` equals `wrap_to_pi(t)` within 1e-9, except at the ±π seam.
- `mean_angle([a, a + d, a - d])` equals `wrap_to_pi(a)` for small `d`.

**Acceptance criteria:** all tests pass, and you can explain the one special case you had to handle for the ±π seam.
